primitives.name: Dixon-Coles τ and ξ
primitives.verbatim_quote: ## Operator cards ### Dixon-Coles τ and ξ — STRUCTURE-ONLY, then TRANSFER on decay Original, soccer, JRSS C 46(2) 265–280: P_DC(x,y) = τ(x,y) Pois(x;λ) Pois(y;μ) τ(0,0)=1-λμρ, τ(1,0)=1+μρ, τ(0,1)=1+λρ, τ(1,1)=1-ρ, else 1.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'x, y': 'score counts (dimensionless)', 'λ, μ': 'expected goals (rate parameters, dimensionless)', 'ρ': 'dependence parameter (dimensionless)', 'τ(x,y)': 'adjustment factor (dimensionless)'}
primitives.assumptions: Poisson process for scoring, bounded dependence via τ adjustment, discrete outcomes.
primitives.breakdown_regime: NFL scores are not 0 and 1, invalidating direct application.

primitives.name: James–Stein / Efron–Morris
primitives.verbatim_quote: James–Stein / Efron–Morris — TRANSFER on rates, banned on the game mean Positive-part: θ̂_i = ν + (1 - (p-2)σ2 / ||Y-ν||2)_+ (Y_i-ν). Efron–Morris: arcsin transform so variance ≈ 1, then shrink. Trains on player EPA, catch rate, NFL success rate, MLB batting, NBA RAPM-style partial pooling.
primitives.assumptions: Normality of estimates, shrinkage towards common mean, partial pooling across leagues.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Banned on game mean due to leakage risk.

layer2.mapping: Enables rate-based shrinkage across sports, transferring to NFL via EPA and success metrics.
layer2.telemetry: Reduction in estimation variance, cross-league consistency.

reasoning_traces.think:
The Dixon-Coles operator is a probabilistic model for football scoring, adjusting Poisson probabilities via a dependence parameter τ. It is structured for soccer but fails when applied directly to NFL due to differing score distributions. The transfer mechanism requires learning decay kernel ξ and adapting τ to NFL-specific constraints. The James–Stein estimator shrinks estimates toward a common mean, useful for pooling across sports but banned on game means to avoid leakage. Its application is restricted to rate-based features like EPA or batting averages. Hawkes processes model temporal excitation, where events trigger future ones. For NFL, these are valid for short-term drives but not for season-wide trends. The model must enforce decay and avoid game-mean leakage. Each operator is vetted by CRPS and walk-forward validation before inclusion.
